meta.title: 8 (stupidly simple) rules to grow on social media
meta.thread_line: 4 threads · who over how many · inner nerd + the five D's · content before packaging · sell a feeling, make 100

snapshot: Shaan Puri's non-obvious creator playbook, built on **100M+ podcast downloads**, ~1M YouTube subscribers and ~500K on Twitter over ~5 years.
**Who follows you beats how many** — 100 Fortune-100 CEOs outweigh 100,000 random readers; Ferrari vs. GM is the business version.
Find your **inner nerd**: the oddly specific obsession eliminates competition and turns success into something you win daily.
Be *known well*, not well known — the **five D's** (done, deliver, do, dreams, dork out) double as a year-long content list.
No such thing as too long, only too boring; ship **A+ content with C- delivery** before polishing packaging.
Early on, build a **binge bank** (one great hour of content); people buy a feeling, not information; then run Mr. Beast's **rule of 100**.
Closing bet: in an AI-content world, the scarce thing is a person who feels real.

themes.title: 100 Fortune-100 CEOs beat 100,000 random readers
themes.lead: Pick the exact audience you care about and accept fewer views if the right people are listening.
bullets: Borrowed from **Tim Ferriss**: would you rather have 100,000 random people read your book, or the 100 CEOs of the Fortune 100? The 100 are worth more.
Example: making sports content for athletes means designing for that specific person, not for likes.

Car analogy: GM sells ~2.5M cars a year and is worth ~$50B; Ferrari sells ~13,000 (about 200x fewer) yet is worth more because its buyers are luxury customers (he said "$80 million" — he means billions).
His own lane is "upmarket", more intelligent content, not mass market — unless mass market is the game you actually want.
Test from the recap: imagine that target person in the chair — could you say this with a straight face, or would they find it "kind of whack"?

quote.text: I'm okay getting less views. I'm okay getting less likes as long as it's the right people and the right likes.

themes.title: Find your inner nerd, then be known well through the five D's
themes.lead: Talk about what you're oddly obsessed with, not what you think the audience wants, and let people know your whole story.
bullets: Advice from his trainer: the best products are a founder pushing a bit of themselves out, "inside out". Ask *what do I nerd out about most?*, not *what does the audience want?*
His uncle's basement model railway with realistic green/yellow signal timing: "biggest dork", but the internet will find the other 1,000-1,000,000 people just as nerdy.
Examples: a woman running **perfume tours** in New York (her nerd is scent); a menswear writer who puts 1,000 words into pant cuffs, hems and cuts.
Payoff 1: almost no competition, "a crowded room, yet you have five feet of space all around you". Payoff 2: success is guaranteed, since playing is winning (odds go from <1% to 100%).
**Five D's**: Done (track record), Deliver (value to followers), Do (work and hobbies), Dreams (e.g. Gary V openly wants to buy the Jets), Dork out (what you collect).
Payoff: connection, plus luck. Followers send deals, recommendations and finds; for him that's niche internet businesses and highly intentional lifestyles, so "every day is like Christmas".
Workflow: spend 10 minutes brainstorming storylines under each D and you have about a year of content pipeline.

quote.text: The goal is not to be well known, it is to be known well.

themes.title: No such thing as too long, and A+ content with C- delivery
themes.lead: Interest sets the length and content comes before production; when numbers are tiny, build an asset instead of watching counts.
bullets: **Joe Rogan**, "the number one podcaster in the world", averages ~3-hour episodes; friends told him to do 22 or 44 minutes to match the average American commute.
If something feels too long, reframe it as too boring and make it more interesting. Content should be as long as it's interesting.
A+ delivery with C- content is a "death trap": hours lost on packaging and post-production instead of finding interesting things to say.

Evidence: sort by oldest. Chris Williamson's early videos; Mr. Beast in his bedroom in a white t-shirt counting to 100,000; Rogan's first episode with After Effects snowflakes and an old webcam. "Find heat first before you find polish."

**Binge bank**: when eight people are viewing, build one binge-worthy hour (6-8 posts, videos or episodes, a "first season") so anyone who binges it walks away asking why nobody is talking about this person.

quote.text: There's no such thing as too long, only too boring.

themes.title: Sell a feeling, make 100 videos, stay real in an AI flood
themes.lead: Fans remember the feeling, not the information; getting good takes 100 reps with one improvement each time.
bullets: He was wrong for a long time: he treated content as information transfer, but even fans struggle to name a favorite episode or something they learned. It goes in one ear and out the other, and a feeling is what's left.
Frame: your channel is a small shop in the world's most crowded flea market, and you sell a feeling.

Feelings sold: **David Blaine** awe (frog swallowing, 18 hours in ice, levitating); **James Clear** self-control; Dana White's UFC "holy moments live on pay-per-view"; Tony Robbins motivation; CrossFit a satisfying sweat ("not the best workout", but addictive).
A feeling once or twice earns a follow; the same feeling every day, more reliably than anywhere else, earns a lifelong fan.

**Mr. Beast's rule of 100** (Puri is a friend): make 100 videos and improve one thing each time (thumbnail, hook, storytelling, color). It filters out the unserious, and the serious won't need advice by video 100. "This is the real algorithm."

Creator culture now feels like "processed food" because big rewards drew the wrong mentality; as AI makes hyper-addictive content, the edge is a person who feels real, e.g. bodybuilder **Sam Sulek** filming workouts "letting you in".
The whole playbook is a concrete version of "just be yourself", advice he calls hollow when given without steps.

quote.text: People do not want information, they want a feeling.

themes.watch: His own reach is the evidence behind the playbook. The Ferrari/GM figures, Rogan's episode length and the Mr. Beast rule are cited from memory and anecdote.

takeaways.title: Name the 100 people you most want following you, and write every piece for them
Spend 10 minutes brainstorming storylines under each of the five D's to fill a year of topics
Ship your first 6-8 pieces as a one-hour binge bank before you look at view counts
Write down the one feeling your work delivers and cut anything that doesn't produce it
Commit to 100 pieces, and pick one element to improve on each

hot_takes.take: There is no such thing as too long, there is only too boring.
You need A+ content with C- delivery... A+ delivery with C- content, that's a death trap.
People do not want information, they want a feeling.
hot_takes.why: Reverses his own earlier view, runs against expertise-first content

hot_takes.take: This rule of a hundred is the real algorithm that you should follow. Forget the news feed.
In a world of AI... what's going to be left is when you bump into a person that feels real.
hot_takes.why: Forward-looking bet on authenticity beating AI content

hot_takes.take: You shift your odds of success from less than 1% to 100%.
hot_takes.why: Numeric claim about the inner-nerd strategy

claims.claim: Making 100 pieces of content and improving one thing each time will make a creator so good they can't be ignored.
As AI produces hyper-addictive content, creators who feel real become the lasting edge.

other_news.title: People cited: Tim Ferriss (100 CEOs framing), Gary Vaynerchuk (Jets dream), Joe Rogan, Chris Williamson, Mr. Beast, David Blaine, James Clear, Dana White/UFC, Tony Robbins, CrossFit, Sam Sulek; the perfume-tour creator was discussed on a past My First Million episode.

glossary.def: The topic you're abnormally obsessed with, used as your content niche instead of guessing what the audience wants.
Done, Deliver, Do, Dreams, Dork out: the five things an audience should know about you to know you well.
An early, roughly one-hour set of content good enough that anyone who binges it becomes a fan.
Mr. Beast's advice: make 100 videos and improve one thing on each.
Prioritize interesting substance over production polish when starting out.
